title: On the phone
job: Calls and messages — openings, closings, taking a message
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: yeoboseyo IS M1'S RULE VISIBLE INSIDE ONE WORD. It is how Korea answers a phone, and it is an honorific imperative of a verb meaning "look here" — yeogi bo- plus -seyo. A learner told that remembers the word AND the rule; a learner given it as an unanalysable noise learns one word. The call then runs on honorifics throughout, which makes this module the payoff of M1's whole decision.

-go isseoyo, THE PROGRESSIVE, opens here, and L1 named it as deferred for exactly this moment: a call is happening NOW. jigeum bap meokgo isseoyo. The -go is L1-M3's own linking ending in a new frame, so nothing new is opened for it. The delta worth stating: Korean's plain -yo present already covers a habitual action, so -go isseoyo is reserved for what is GENUINELY IN PROGRESS — the same restriction en-it puts on its gerundio, where en-fr and en-de have no progressive at all.

Absence uses the negation the course already owns: an gyeseyo — literally "is not honourably present" — which is how a Korean office says somebody is not in. The honorific STAYS in the negative and stays even about somebody absent, because it is about the person and not the situation.

jamsiman-yo is the hold, and it is a NOUN with -yo stuck on the end. That is worth its own line: -yo politens a fragment, not only a verb, which is why Korean can be polite in two syllables where English needs a clause.

Taking a message needs no new tense — memo, jeonhwa beonho, and L1-M5's past. -l-geyo (najunge jeonhwahalgeyo, "I'll call later") is a PROMISE ending built on L1-M6's -l shape and is taught as one item, not as a system. Reported speech (-dago) is L3's, which is why a message here is passed on with the words themselves.

words.note: An honorific imperative meaning 'look here' — M1's ending frozen into a greeting. It is used on the telephone and almost nowhere else.
L1-M1's jeo with the copula. Korean identifies itself with 'I am' where English says 'it is me', and the vowel ending takes -yeyo.

sentences.trap: yeoboseyo belongs to the telephone. Said to somebody in front of you it is either a joke or a way of getting the attention of a stranger, and neither is what a learner intends.
sentences.sound: YEO-bo-se-yo, JEO-ye-yo. Four even syllables and then three.

variations.changed: answering, with the rise that asks who is there
naming who you hope has answered

mistake.why: A phone is answered with yeoboseyo: Yeoboseyo, jeoyeyo.

sentences.usage: Both ends of a Korean call open with it.
sentences.mnemonic: 'Look here' — an imperative that became a hello.

words.note: The commonest Korean surname by a long way, and a surname goes FIRST — Kim seonsaengnim, never seonsaengnim Kim. With a given name L1-M1's -ssi does the same job: Yuna-ssi, Minsu-ssi.

sentences.trap: gyeseyo and not isseoyo, because the person asked after is honoured. M2 opened the separate honorific verb for existence, and a phone call is where it is used ten times a day.
sentences.sound: kim seon-saeng-NIM gye-SE-yo. gye is one syllable.

mistake.why: An honoured person takes gyeseyo: Kim seonsaengnim gyeseyo?

sentences.usage: Asking to be put through, in an office or a home.
sentences.mnemonic: The surname goes first. The honorific stays.

words.note: The word that pins a sentence to this moment, and it is what -go isseoyo usually travels with. It goes at the front.

sentences.trap: The honorific stays even in the negative and even about somebody who is not there. It is about the PERSON, not about the situation, and dropping it because they are absent is the mistake to avoid.
sentences.sound: JI-geum an gye-SE-yo. an is short and unstressed.

variations.changed: with what to do about it
L1-M4's today, so a whole day
the answer that puts you through

mistake.why: The honorific stays in the negative: Jigeum an gyeseyo.

sentences.usage: What you hear when the person you want is out.
sentences.mnemonic: Honour the person, not the situation.

words.note: L1-M3's linking -go plus L1-M3's isseoyo — 'doing and being at it'. Reserved for what is genuinely in progress, because the plain -yo already covers a habit.

sentences.trap: meogeoyo already means both 'eats' and 'is eating'. -go isseoyo is not the ordinary present; it is the emphatic one, used when the fact that it is happening right now is the point — which on a phone it usually is.
sentences.sound: JI-geum bap MEOK-go i-SSEO-yo. The k of meokgo hardens the g after it.

variations.cue: He's on the phone right now.

variations.changed: the plain present, which covers the habit

mistake.why: The progressive takes -go: Jigeum bap meokgo isseoyo.

sentences.usage: Explaining why somebody cannot come to the phone.
sentences.mnemonic: -go isseoyo is for NOW. -yo is for usually.

words.note: A NOUN with -yo stuck on it — jamsi, a moment, plus -man, only. -yo politens a fragment and not only a verb, which is how Korean is polite in two syllables.

sentences.trap: -yo does not need a verb under it. That is why Korean can politen a single word — jamsiman-yo, yeogi-yo — where English needs a whole clause to do the same work.
sentences.sound: jam-si-MAN-yo. The n runs into the yo and is heard as nyo.

variations.changed: the full request, with M1's fused form

mistake.why: Dropping the -yo drops the politeness: Jamsiman-yo.

sentences.usage: Putting somebody on hold, or squeezing past them in a shop.
sentences.mnemonic: -yo politens a fragment, not just a verb.

words.note: The noun, and jeonhwahaeyo is the verb built straight on it with hada — Korean makes hundreds of verbs that way, and ilhago is L1-M4's work doing the same.
A number in the sense of a label — a phone number, a room number — and never a quantity. A phone number is read digit by digit with Sino numbers.
'Becomes'. eotteoke dwaeyo — 'how does it turn out' — is the polite way to ask for a detail, softer than mwoyeyo.

sentences.trap: eotteoke dwaeyo — literally 'how does it become' — is the polite way to ask for a detail, and it is softer than mwoyeyo. Korean asks how something turns out rather than what it is.
sentences.sound: JEON-hwa BEON-ho-ga eo-TTEO-ke DWAE-yo. dwaeyo rhymes with English 'dway'.

variations.changed: asked for outright, with M1's request
L1-M1's name, in the same polite frame
asking whether there is one at all

mistake.why: A detail is asked politely with eotteoke dwaeyo: Jeonhwa beonho-ga eotteoke dwaeyo?

sentences.usage: Taking down a number, and the polite form matters here.
sentences.mnemonic: Korean asks how it BECOMES, not what it is.

words.note: From the English word. It is what an office takes when somebody is out, and it goes with namgida, to leave behind.
namgyeo- plus M1's juseyo, the same fusion as dowajuseyo and gidaryeojuseyo. One token, no space, no hyphen.

sentences.trap: This is M1's request pattern doing ordinary office work. Nothing about it is idiomatic — once the -a/eo juseyo fusion is understood, dozens of sentences like it build themselves.
sentences.sound: ME-mo-reul nam-GYEO-joo-se-yo. The gyeo is one syllable.

variations.changed: the plain request, which is what an office says
the number rather than a message

mistake.why: A request takes juseyo: Memo-reul namgyeojuseyo.

sentences.usage: Said by whoever answered, before you have to ask.
sentences.mnemonic: -a/eo juseyo builds itself, once you have it.

words.note: Later in the same day or later in general, and it already contains L1-M7's -e. It goes at the front, like every time word.
A PROMISE, not a prediction: it says what the speaker undertakes to do. L1-M6's -l geoyeyo simply states a plan, and only -l-geyo commits.

sentences.trap: -l-geyo COMMITS where L1-M6's -l geoyeyo only states a plan. And it is first person only: you cannot promise on somebody else's behalf, and Korean grammar refuses to let you try.
sentences.sound: na-JUNG-e jeon-hwa-HAL-ge-yo. The g of -geyo is hardened by the l in front of it.
sentences.usage: Closing a call you will have to finish another time.

words.note: L1-M5's past on the hada verb. Nothing new is opened for it: -eoss- is L1's, and this is one more cell of it.

sentences.trap: A message is passed on with the words themselves at this level. Reported speech — 'he said that he would call' — needs -dago, which belongs to L3 and is deliberately not here.
sentences.sound: EO-je jeon-hwa-HAE-sseo-yo. The sseo is tense.

variations.changed: as a question, with a rise
naming who, with the subject particle

mistake.why: A past time word needs the past: Eoje jeonhwahaesseoyo.

sentences.usage: Reporting a call that already happened.
sentences.mnemonic: -eoss- is L1's. Every past is one of its cells.

words.note: L1-M2's farewell, and a call is where it is easiest: the other person is staying where they are, so it is gyeseyo and never gaseyo.

sentences.trap: Korean has two goodbyes and the caller uses the STAYING one, because the person at the other end is not going anywhere. L1-M2 taught both; a phone is where the choice finally has an obvious answer.
sentences.sound: ne, an-NYEONG-hi gye-SE-yo. The hi is light.

mistake.why: The one on the other end is staying: Ne, annyeonghi gyeseyo.

sentences.usage: Closing a call — and the choice of goodbye is not free.
sentences.mnemonic: They are not going anywhere. So gyeseyo.
